argument_macro_structure.dominant_argument_form: Reconciliation of apparent contradiction through distinction-making and hierarchical derivation
argument_macro_structure.premise_explicitness: High - premises are stated as principles and distinctions, with textual citations

argumentative_quality.dialectical_reasonableness: Strong - anticipates and resolves objections by distinguishing cases
argumentative_quality.logical_relevance: High - all sections directly address the alleged contradiction
argumentative_quality.premise_acceptability: Moderate - relies on contested interpretations of Socratic moral psychology and political theory

distinctions_drawn: divine mandate (positive duty to do just act) vs political obligation (duty to suffer penalty)
explicit_definitions_given: nomos: constitutional, rational, just order of the city
kratos: power, specifically illegitimate factional rule
divine mandate: command to pursue wisdom and virtue (philosophy)
political obligation: duty to obey laws grounded in social contract and non-maleficence

dialectical_engagement.objection_handling: Uses the Thirty Tyrants anecdote as the central objection and turns it into evidence for the unified framework
objections_raised: If Socrates must obey the laws in the Crito, why did he disobey the Thirty Tyrants?
If Socrates must obey the god in the Apology, why does he obey the court in the Crito?

named_thought_experiments: Hypothetical law commanding Socrates to stop philosophizing
Thirty Tyrants' order to arrest Leon of Salamis

philosophical_orientation.grounding: Deontological - justice as absolute prohibition on injustice
philosophical_orientation.sentiment: Rationalist - reason and moral integrity as supreme
philosophical_orientation.thematic_focus: Political obligation, civil disobedience, moral integrity, divine command vs legal authority

structural_organization.structure_type: Thesis-driven with numbered sections and cumulative argumentation

summary_of_core_decisions: The text resolves the apparent contradiction by distinguishing between commands that require unjust action and penalties that only require suffering. Socrates' absolute principle is never to commit injustice; therefore he must disobey unjust commands (Apology, Thirty Tyrants) but obey just penalties (Crito). His commitment is to the nomos, not to any regime, and the divine mandate to philosophize is itself a just activity subordinate to the same principle.

thesis_commitment.hedging_density_in_final_paragraph: Low - final paragraph is assertive and celebratory
